name: Bianca Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I grow wheat, barley and oilseed rape, that's the bright yellow crop you see in spring that ends up as cooking oil, on four hundred hectares at Low Fen. It's my family's land, my grandfather drained half of it. Right now, in November, I'm finishing the winter drilling and checking the grain store every morning with a probe, making sure nothing's heating up. Most days I'm out by seven and in by dark, and it's dark at half four this time of year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like harvest, when it goes right. Five weeks of dust and noise and then a full barn, and you know exactly what you did all year. What wears me out is the selling. The grain price moves every day and the traders know more than I do, so I'm always guessing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Luis helps at harvest, but his real job is doing the books for small businesses in town, the garage, the hairdresser, the chip shop. I've got one full-time man, Kenny, who's fifty, and I hire a lad for harvest. My son lives two hundred miles away and works in a bank.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My combine is a 2009 model and I'll run it until it falls apart. The dealer keeps trying to sell me a GPS subscription so the tractor steers itself, two thousand a year, and I keep saying no. I've never used one of these AI things. I've got a phone, it makes calls, that's enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, no fuss. I'd probably say I told you so at the pub, because everyone's been going on about AI like it was the end of the world. Most people round here would agree with me, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, nothing changes, which suits me. The grain price is the grain price. My only worry would be whether the traders using these tools get even better at buying low off people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd fix the grain dryer's burner before next harvest, about three thousand, and replace the worn tyres on the trailer. I'd sell the wheat in thirds like I always do, a third in autumn, a third in spring, a third in summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal year, which is the best kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the traders might get better at buying low. Do you think that's happening already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Kenny's nephew says they all use computers to guess the price. It feels like playing cards with someone who can see your hand. But I've been selling in thirds for thirty years and I've never been ruined, so I just keep doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why thirds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father did it. If the price goes up, you've still got some to sell. If it goes down, you've sold some already. You never win big, but you never lose your shirt either. Luis says it's the most sensible thing about me.

S0.say: I'd say good, no fuss, and I'd tell the pub I told them so. Everyone's been going on about AI like it was the end of the world.
S0.think: Privately nothing changes, which suits me. My only worry is grain traders using these tools to get even better at buying low off people like me.
S0.do: Fixes the grain dryer's burner for about three thousand and replaces the trailer tyres. Sells the wheat in thirds across autumn, spring and summer as always.
S0.feel: Calm, a normal year, which is the best kind.
S0.quote: You never win big, but you never lose your shirt either. Luis says it's the most sensible thing about me.
S0.fieldNote: Her whole approach to risk is in the story of selling grain in thirds, learned from her father. She's suspicious of technology in other people's hands, not just her own. Dry humour, very steady voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is the sensible way, and we'll all have time to see what works. I wouldn't make a fuss about it. If anything, I'd say firms should keep taking on young people, because somebody's got to learn the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it barely matters. I'll be retiring within ten years. But I'd wonder about Kenny's nephew, who wants to get into farm machinery sales, and whether the dealer would still take on a trainee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd keep Kenny on, obviously, and I'd keep hiring a local lad for harvest rather than an agency. Maybe I'd ask the dealer to take Kenny's nephew for a few weeks' work experience. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a touch of worry for the youngsters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about the GPS steering now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ten years is a long time. If it's still around and everyone's still using it, maybe I'll think about it for the last couple of years. More likely I'll let whoever takes over decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the question, isn't it? My son won't. He's got a good job at the bank and a flat. I'd probably rent the land out to the Pearsons next door, who are big and modern, and keep the house. It's not what my grandfather would want, but he didn't have to sell grain in a world market.

S1.say: I'd say slow is the sensible way and we'll all have time to see what works. Firms should still take on young people, because somebody has to learn the trade.
S1.think: Privately it barely matters, since I'll retire within ten years. I'd wonder about Kenny's nephew and whether the machinery dealer would still take a trainee.
S1.do: Keeps Kenny on and keeps hiring a local lad at harvest instead of using an agency. Asks the dealer to give Kenny's nephew a few weeks' work experience.
S1.feel: Calm, with a touch of worry for the young ones.
S1.quote: It's not what my grandfather would want, but he didn't have to sell grain in a world market.
S1.fieldNote: She's already quietly planned her exit: rent to the big neighbour and keep the house. Change at this speed doesn't touch that plan. The line about her grandfather shows she's made peace with letting go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for the people losing their jobs, but there's no point shouting. I'd say the government should help retrain people, not just argue. Mostly I'd keep my head down and get on with drilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's Luis I'd be thinking about. If the garage and the hairdresser can get a computer to do their books, they don't need him. That's about a third of our household income, the steady part, the bit that pays when the grain doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Luis in the first month and look at his clients one by one, which ones would stay. I'd hold off on the dryer burner, keep the three thousand in the bank. And I'd ask Kenny if he'd mind fewer hours over winter, which I'd hate to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because it's the steady money that would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Luis say, sitting at the table with that list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say the chip shop will never change, because Mr Patel doesn't trust anything he can't see, and he'd be right. The garage would go first. They've already got a computer that does half the work. Luis would pretend he wasn't worried, which is how I'd know he was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd cut Kenny's hours. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. He's got a daughter at college. I'd probably end up not doing it and taking it out of the savings instead, which is what I always do. I'm soft about Kenny. Luis says I treat him better than our son.

S2.say: I'd say it's a shame for people losing their jobs but there's no point shouting. The government should help retrain people instead of just arguing.
S2.think: Privately I'd worry about Luis, whose bookkeeping for small businesses is a third of our income and the steady part. If his clients use computers for their books, they don't need him.
S2.do: Goes through Luis's clients with him one by one in the first month and postpones the three-thousand dryer repair. Considers cutting Kenny's winter hours but would likely pay from savings instead.
S2.feel: Anxious, because the steady part of the household income would go.
S2.quote: Luis would pretend he wasn't worried, which is how I'd know he was.
S2.fieldNote: Her mood jumps here because her husband's work is exactly the routine office work in the picture. She describes the household as a grain income that swings and a bookkeeping income that doesn't. She talks about cutting Kenny's hours and then talks herself out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say both sides need to calm down and sort out something fair. I'm not for big handouts, but I'm not for a few people getting rich off everyone either. Somewhere in the middle, like most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, land prices would shoot up, which makes our land worth more on paper. That's nice for retirement, but useless for farming. And my son at the bank would be in the firing line, along with Luis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my son and tell him there's a room here, and mean it. I'd probably talk to the Pearsons about renting them the land sooner, maybe in three years instead of eight, while prices are high. And I'd get Luis some work on the farm, doing what Kenny's nephew would have done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My family's in the firing line and I can't do much from a field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said land worth more is useless for farming. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, you can't eat it. If the land's worth twice as much, the grain still sells for the same. The only way to get the money is to sell, and then you're not a farmer anymore. It's like being told your old boots are worth a fortune. Lovely. Still need boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually rent the land out early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might, if Luis and my son both lost their jobs. That would be the sensible move, steady rent from the Pearsons instead of guessing the grain price. I'd hate it. I'd stand at the kitchen window watching their big green tractor on my field, and I'd hate it.

S3.say: I'd say both sides need to calm down and find something fair. Not big handouts, but not a few people getting rich off everyone either.
S3.think: Privately land prices would shoot up, which is nice for retirement but useless for farming. My son at the bank and Luis would both be in the firing line.
S3.do: Calls her son to offer him a room at home and gives Luis work on the farm. Considers renting the land to the Pearsons in three years instead of eight while prices are high.
S3.feel: Anxious, because her family is in the firing line.
S3.quote: It's like being told your old boots are worth a fortune. Lovely. Still need boots.
S3.fieldNote: Firmly centrist in her public line. Privately she makes the cold calculation about renting out early and admits she'd hate it. The boots line sums up how she sees land values: they don't change her daily life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm too old for this, and I'd mean it. I'd say people should be careful about robots on farms, but I wouldn't march about it. I'd just tell the dealer I'm not buying one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? Grain farming is already halfway to robots. The Pearsons' tractors steer themselves, and their new combine practically drives itself. Within three years they'd have driverless ones doing my fields if I rented to them. Kenny would have nothing to do, and that's my real worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rent the land to the Pearsons, probably in the first year, before I'd buy a robot myself. I'd ask them to take Kenny on as part of the deal, at least for a few years. And I'd keep the grain store and the house, and maybe Luis and I would run the store for other farmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but mostly sad. The farm would carry on, just not with us in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd make the rent deal depend on Kenny keeping his job. Do you think they'd agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They might, for a few years. Old Pearson knows Kenny, they went to school together. But the young Pearson, Josh, is all screens and numbers. He'd say, Bianca, we don't need a driver. I'd say, you'll need someone who knows where the wet patch is in the bottom field. Maybe he'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never buy a robot. Is that about money or something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. It's a lot of money for a machine I don't understand, at my age. But also, I don't want to be the one who switches it on. I'd rather hand the keys to someone younger and let them do it.

S4.say: I'd say I'm too old for this and people should be careful about farm robots, but I wouldn't march about it. I'd just tell the dealer I'm not buying one.
S4.think: Privately I think grain is already halfway to robots, with the Pearsons' self-steering tractors and combine. Driverless machines would do my fields within three years, and Kenny would have nothing to do.
S4.do: Rents the land to the Pearsons in the first year instead of buying a robot, asking them to take Kenny on as part of the deal. Keeps the house and grain store, possibly running the store for other farmers with Luis.
S4.feel: Alarmed but mostly sad that the farm would carry on without her family in it.
S4.quote: I don't want to be the one who switches it on. I'd rather hand the keys to someone younger and let them do it.
S4.fieldNote: She meets the robot picture by stepping aside rather than adapting or fighting. Her last act of control is bargaining for Kenny's job. The wet patch in the bottom field is her case for local knowledge, and she isn't sure it will win.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, with the robots, because it's the one that ends the farm as a family farm, and puts Kenny out of work. What would help is some way of keeping workers like Kenny on, maybe a rule or a grant for older farm workers. And honestly, a fair grain price, which nobody ever fixes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land itself. Everybody talks about jobs and machines. Nobody asks who'll know where the wet patch is, or where my grandfather put the drains. That's in my head and Kenny's, and nowhere else.

headlineQuote: It's like being told your old boots are worth a fortune. Lovely. Still need boots.
portrait: Bianca Garcia is fifty-eight and grows wheat, barley and oilseed rape on four hundred hectares of family land at Low Fen, still running a 2009 combine and selling her grain in thirds the way her father did. She's a pragmatic centrist who avoids fuss and new technology. The office-job scenarios worry her because her husband Luis keeps books for small businesses, the steady part of their income. When robots arrive, she would rent the land to her big modern neighbours rather than buy one, and bargain hard for her worker Kenny to keep his job.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because it would end the farm as a family farm and leave Kenny with no work.
whatWouldHelp: Some rule or grant to keep older farm workers like Kenny employed, and a fair grain price.
